etymology: From the old intensive prefix be- joined to take (Saxon tacan, to lay hold of); hence to betake oneself, to take one’s own self away to a place, to have recourse, to resort, to flee for shelter. Always reflexive — a man betakes himself.
biblical_def: To betake is to take oneself somewhere — and the grammar preaches. The verb will not take an object but the man himself; he does not betake his goods or his opinions, he betakes himself. It is the word for recourse, for resort, for the whole person fleeing to a shelter he has judged safe. The Authorized translators put it in their own margin at Isa 14:32, where the text reads, “the poor of his people shall trust in it,” and the margin offers, or, betake themselves unto it — for the Hebrew chāsāh means to take shelter, to run under a covert. That margin is a whole doctrine of faith. Faith is not an estimate formed at a distance; it is a betaking. David knew it: “in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge” (Psa 57:1); “I flee unto thee to hide me” (Psa 143:9). Boaz blessed Ruth as one who had come under the wings of the God of Israel to trust (Rut 2:12). David, hunted, “escaped to the cave Adullam” (1Sa 22:1), and the man of God under the covenant does the same with his soul. The epistle to the Hebrews gathers it up: we are they “who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us” (Heb 6:18). The fleeing and the laying hold are one act. Christ is the covert; to believe on Him is to betake oneself to Him and stay.
webster_summary: To take one’s self to; to have recourse; to resort or flee to for shelter.
webster_full: BETAKE, to take to; to have recourse to; to apply; to resort; with the reciprocal pronoun.
From be- + take (Saxon tacan, to lay hold of).
It is used reflexively: a man betakes himself to a refuge or to a work.
The AV margin renders Isa 14:32 betake themselves unto it for “trust.”
The Hebrew behind it, chāsāh, means to take shelter under a covert.
scriptures: What shall one then answer the messengers of the nation? That the LORD hath founded Zion, and the poor of his people shall trust in it.
Deliver me, O LORD, from mine enemies: I flee unto thee to hide me.
Heb 6:18
That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:
Rut 2:12
The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
corruption_summary: An archaic reflexive that guarded a truth our age has lost: faith is not an opinion held but a self committed.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has faded from ordinary speech, and with it a grammar that once kept faith honest. Modern religion speaks of belief as a position a man occupies: he holds a view, he identifies with a tradition, he accepts a proposition about God and leaves himself where he was. The old verb will not permit it. Betaking is reflexive; the man goes where his faith goes. The refugee who admires the city of refuge from the road outside its gate is as dead as if he had never heard of it; the avenger of blood does not respect an opinion. So the Scripture never asks whether a man esteems the covert highly, but whether he is under it: “the poor of his people shall trust in it” — shall betake themselves unto it.

The recovery is the Reformed doctrine of saving faith itself: notitia, assensus, and fiducia — knowledge, assent, and trust — where the third is the betaking, the whole soul casting itself upon Christ and resting there. Devils have the first two and tremble (Jas 2:19). And because the flight is a flight, it is a work God must give: the effectual call is the LORD bringing the sinner off the road and under the wings. Yet the invitation stands to every man who hears it, and the shelter is never crowded. He that betakes himself to Christ finds two immutable things — God’s promise and God’s oath — already holding him fast before ever he laid hold on them.
roots_summary: To take one’s self away to a refuge; the reflexive verb of flight and recourse.
roots_lines: Betake — be- (intensive) + take, “to lay hold of.”
Always reflexive: a man betakes himself, never a thing.
It renders the sense of Hebrew chāsāh, to take shelter under a covert.
The AV margin at Isa 14:32 reads betake themselves unto it.
Hebrews calls believers those who “fled for refuge” (Heb 6:18).
usage: He betook himself to the cave: David’s body did what faith does with the soul.
Faith is a betaking, not an estimate formed at a safe distance.
The margin of the Authorized Version turns a preposition into a doctrine: betake themselves unto it.

etymology: From the Saxon lāþian, “to hate, to be hateful,” from lāþ, “hateful, odious”; hence to feel disgust at, to abhor, to turn from with nausea of soul. The AV also spells it lothe.
biblical_def: To loathe is to abhor with disgust — not cool dislike but the soul turning from a thing with nausea. Scripture uses the word two ways, and the difference between them is the difference between damnation and repentance. First, men loathe what God gives. In the wilderness the people spake against God and against Moses, “and our soul loatheth this light bread” (Num 21:5) — the manna, bread from heaven, corn of angels, rained daily upon ingratitude. Solomon explains the palate: “The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet” (Pro 27:7). Fulness is the enemy of relish, and a soul stuffed with the world will gag on grace. Second, and this is the mercy, men loathe themselves. Ezekiel is the prophet of it: “ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed” (Eze 20:43); and again, “shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations” (Eze 36:31). Mark where the word falls in that chapter: after the new heart and the new spirit, after the sprinkling of clean water. Self-loathing for sin is not the cause of God’s mercy but its fruit; the man who sees the clean water is the man who at last sees the filth. Job says it plainly in the dust: “I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:6). So the manna-loather perishes and the self-loather lives.
webster_summary: To feel disgust at; to abhor; to turn from with nausea of body or of soul.
webster_full: LOATHE, to feel disgust at; to have an extreme aversion of the appetite to food or drink.
Also, to hate; to dislike greatly; to abhor.
From Saxon lāþian, from lāþ, “hateful, odious.”
Israel’s soul loathed the manna, the bread of heaven (Num 21:5).
Ezekiel foretells the penitent loathing himself in his own sight (Eze 36:31).
scriptures: Num 21:5

And the people spake against God, and against Moses, Wherefore have ye brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? for there is no bread, neither is there any water; and our soul loatheth this light bread.
And there shall ye remember your ways, and all your doings, wherein ye have been defiled; and ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for all your evils that ye have committed.
Then shall ye remember your own evil ways, and your doings that were not good, and shall lothe yourselves in your own sight for your iniquities and for your abominations.
Pro 27:7
The full soul loatheth an honeycomb; but to the hungry soul every bitter thing is sweet.
corruption_summary: The age has abolished self-loathing as a category and calls the abolition healing; Scripture calls the loathing of sin the first honest sight a man ever has of himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic creed of our day holds that a man’s central problem is a low view of himself, and that the cure is to raise it — to esteem, accept, and validate the self as it stands. On that creed Ezekiel’s promise reads as a curse: ye shall lothe yourselves in your own sight. But the creed is false at its root, because it mistakes the disease. The sinner’s ruin is not that he thinks too little of himself; it is that he loves himself supremely and God not at all, and every counsel that feeds that love feeds the ruin. Scripture never asks a man to invent a bad opinion of himself; it asks him to receive a true one. The publican who would not lift his eyes went down to his house justified, and the Pharisee who esteemed himself well went home condemned (Luk 18:13–14). What the age calls a wound is, in Ezekiel, the sign that the new heart has been given.

Yet the doctrine cuts the other way too, and the corruption has a second face: a brooding, unbelieving self-hatred that never comes to Christ, that gnaws at itself and calls the gnawing repentance. That is not Ezekiel’s loathing either, for his stands in a chapter of clean water, new heart, and a new spirit — the loathing of a pardoned man looking back. Godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation, not to be repented of; the sorrow of the world worketh death (2Co 7:10). And the deepest cure of the false appetite is the true one: the full soul loathes the honeycomb, so the LORD empties His people that manna may taste like manna again. Hunger for Christ is the end of loathing Him.
roots_summary: To abhor with disgust — of the manna by the ungrateful, and of self by the penitent.
roots_lines: Loathe — Saxon lāþian, “to hate,” from lāþ, “odious.”
AV also spells the verb lothe (Eze 20:43; 36:31).
Israel loathed the manna — ingratitude gagging on grace (Num 21:5).
Fulness breeds loathing; hunger makes bitter things sweet (Pro 27:7).
Evangelical self-loathing follows the new heart; it does not purchase it.
usage: Our soul loatheth this light bread: the murmurer’s verdict on bread from heaven.
Ezekiel’s penitent loathes himself after the clean water, not before it.
The full soul loathes the honeycomb — a warning to every well-fed church.

etymology: The older aphetic form of establish, from Old French establir, from Latin stabilire, “to make firm,” from stabilis, “standing fast,” from stare, “to stand.” To make stable; to fix; to settle so that a thing cannot be moved.
biblical_def: To stablish is to make a thing stand — to fix, settle, and secure it so that it holds. The Authorized Version keeps the older short form beside establish, and it falls most often on the doctrine our age most needs. Note who does the stablishing. Paul prays “to the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God” (1Th 3:13); he asks that God “comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work” (2Th 2:17); he blesses the One “that is of power to stablish you according to my gospel” (Rom 16:25); he says flatly, “he which stablisheth us with you in Christ…is God” (2Co 1:21). Peter says the same after the furnace: “the God of all grace…after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you” (1Pe 5:10). Four verbs, one Actor. The believer’s perseverance is not the strength of his grip upon Christ but the strength of Christ’s grip upon him; the saints continue because God stablishes, and God stablishes because He has covenanted to do it. So the psalmist prays for the ground of it: “Stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear” (Psa 119:38). The word stablishes the man because God stablishes the word; and the throne of David’s greater Son is stablished for ever (2Sa 7:13).
webster_summary: To make firm or stable; to fix; to settle; to confirm so that a thing cannot be moved.
webster_full: STABLISH, to fix; to settle in a state for permanence; to make firm.
The aphetic older form of establish; the AV uses both.
From Latin stabilire, from stabilis, “standing fast” (stare, to stand).
In the epistles God is nearly always the One who stablishes (2Co 1:21).
Peter joins it to perfecting, strengthening, and settling (1Pe 5:10).
scriptures: To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.
Comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work.
But the God of all grace, who hath called us unto his eternal glory by Christ Jesus, after that ye have suffered a while, make you perfect, stablish, strengthen, settle you.
Stablish thy word unto thy servant, who is devoted to thy fear.
corruption_summary: The word is passive in the saint and active in God; modern religion reverses it and hands the believer the job of holding on.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet at this word. The first is the free-will revivalism that makes perseverance a task laid on the convert: he must keep himself, maintain his decision, hold his ground, and if he slips the whole work collapses. On that scheme a Christian is stablished only as long as his nerve lasts, and assurance is impossible by definition. The second error is the mirror image — a bare “once saved, always saved” that severs the promise from the process, as though a man could be stablished without ever standing, secured without ever being sanctified. Scripture will have neither. It says God stablishes, and it says the stablished walk in every good word and work; the same passage holds both because the God who ordains the end ordains the means.

The Reformed answer is the perseverance of the saints, and it is only the doctrine of these verses read plainly. Peter puts the suffering first and the stablishing after — after that ye have suffered a while — because God’s ordinary way of making a soul stand is to knock out every prop but Himself. Paul asks that hearts be stablished unblameable in holiness at the coming of Christ, which is to say that the saint’s final standing is already the object of an apostolic prayer God has bound Himself to answer. The believer’s comfort is therefore not in the firmness of his hold but in the faithfulness of the Holder: “the foundation of God standeth sure” (2Ti 2:19), and He that began a good work will perform it.
roots_summary: To make firm and unmoveable; in the epistles, always God’s work upon His people.
roots_lines: Stablish — older form of establish, Latin stabilire, “to make firm.”
The root is stare, “to stand” — a stablished man stands.
God is the subject: He stablisheth us in Christ (2Co 1:21).
It sits beside perfect, strengthen, settle in 1Pe 5:10.
The Word stablishes the servant because God stablishes the Word (Psa 119:38).
usage: He may stablish your hearts: the praying apostle asks God for what no convert can do for himself.
Stablish, strengthen, settle — three words for one covenant faithfulness.
A saint stands, but he does not stand by standing; he stands because God stablishes.

etymology: From Latin provocare, “to call forth, to challenge” (pro-, forth, + vocare, to call). The root sense is neutral — to call something out of a man — and the AV keeps both the evil sense (calling forth wrath) and the good (calling forth love).
biblical_def: To provoke is to call a thing forth out of another — and what is called forth may be wrath or may be love. The Authorized Version holds both senses, and the second is the surprise. In the darker sense, provocation is Israel’s besetting history: “They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger” (Deu 32:16); “they have provoked me to anger with their vanities” (Deu 32:21). The Psalms rehearse it and Hebrews warns the church by it. Fathers may do it to their children: “ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath” (Eph 6:4) — a word that binds the head of the house, whose authority is real and whose provocations are therefore weighty. Charity itself is described by its refusal to be baited: love “is not easily provoked” (1Co 13:5). But then the Spirit takes the word and sanctifies it: “let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works” (Heb 10:24). Here provocation becomes a Christian duty and a means of grace. The saints are to study one another — consider is a word of deliberate attention — and then to needle, stir, and call forth in each other the very graces the flesh would leave sleeping. Paul knew the practice: the zeal of Achaia “hath provoked very many” (2Co 9:2). A sluggish church is not provoked enough.
webster_summary: To call forth; to excite or stir up — to anger, or, in the good sense, to love and good works.
webster_full: PROVOKE, to call into action; to arouse; to excite.
Also, to make angry; to offend; to incense; to enrage.
From Latin provocare, pro- (forth) + vocare (to call).
The AV uses it of provoking God to anger (Deu 32:16) …
… and of provoking the brethren unto love and good works (Heb 10:24).
scriptures: They provoked him to jealousy with strange gods, with abominations provoked they him to anger.
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
For I know the forwardness of your mind, for which I boast of you to them of Macedonia, that Achaia was ready a year ago; and your zeal hath provoked very many.
corruption_summary: Modern manners have made provocation a sin in itself, so the church has lost the duty of Heb 10:24 along with the vice of Deu 32.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has collapsed into one sense. To provoke now means simply to offend, and a man who provokes is guilty by definition; the highest congregational virtue becomes leaving one another undisturbed. So the church loses a command. Heb 10:24 does not ask believers to tolerate one another at a distance; it tells them to consider one another — to watch a brother closely enough to know which grace is asleep in him — and then to provoke it awake. That is what the assembling of ourselves together is for, and the verse that follows says so. A congregation where no one is ever stirred, never asked why he has left off the means of grace, never shamed out of sloth by another man’s zeal, is not a peaceable congregation; it is a congregation that has quietly agreed to let each other alone on the way to judgment.

The evil sense must be kept just as sharply, because the age has lost that too. Deu 32 says the living God is provoked — not ruffled, for He is impassible and unchanging in His blessedness, but truly and justly moved against sin in the way Scripture ascribes to Him. Idolatry is not a private taste; it is a provocation of the Almighty, and the modern conviction that God is too kind to be angered is itself the deepest provocation of all. Fathers must hear it in their own sphere: authority that exasperates rather than nurtures calls forth wrath in a child’s heart, and the same apostle who commands children to obey binds the father not to give them cause. Provoke to love; never to wrath.
roots_summary: To call forth — wrath, when God or a child is provoked; love and good works, when a brother is.
roots_lines: Provoke — Latin provocare, “to call forth, challenge.”
The root is morally neutral; the object decides the sense.
Israel provoked the LORD to jealousy and to anger (Deu 32:16, 21).
Fathers are forbidden to provoke their children to wrath (Eph 6:4).
Believers are commanded to provoke one another unto love (Heb 10:24).
usage: Provoke unto love and to good works — the only command in Scripture to stir up a brother.
They provoked him to anger with their vanities: idolatry is a challenge flung at heaven.
Charity is not easily provoked, but charity is diligent to provoke.

etymology: From the Saxon seōþan, “to boil,” cognate with the German sieden; hence to boil, to decoct in liquor. The past participle sodden is the same word, and survives in the AV (Exo 12:9).
biblical_def: To seethe is to boil — to cook flesh in liquid, as opposed to roasting it in fire. It is a kitchen word that Scripture makes a covenant word. Thrice the law forbids one particular boiling: “Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother’s milk” (Exo 23:19; cf. Exo 34:26; Deu 14:21). The prohibition stands attached to the firstfruits, and its logic is the logic of the whole ceremonial law: the milk given to nourish the kid’s life must not be turned into the broth of its death. What God ordained for life may not be conscripted for slaughter. Whether the practice was also a Canaanite fertility rite, the ground the LORD gives is His own: “for thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God” (Deu 14:21). Holiness reaches to the pot. Elsewhere the word is domestic and plain. Manna was to be prepared before the sabbath — “bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe” (Exo 16:23) — the LORD provided for His rest before He commanded it. Elisha bids his servant, “Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets” (2Ki 4:38), and death in the pot is healed by meal cast in at the prophet’s word. And Zechariah ends the age with it: every pot in Jerusalem shall be holiness unto the LORD, and the worshippers shall come and seethe therein (Zec 14:21) — the last kitchen made a sanctuary.
webster_summary: To boil; to decoct or prepare in hot liquor; the past participle is sodden.
webster_full: SEETHE, to boil; to decoct or prepare for food in hot liquor.
Also intransitive: to be in a state of ebullition; to boil.
From Saxon seōþan, to boil; cognate with German sieden.
The old participle sodden is retained in the AV (Exo 12:9).
The law thrice forbids seething a kid in his mother’s milk.
scriptures: The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.

Ye shall not eat of any thing that dieth of itself: thou shalt give it unto the stranger that is in thy gates, that he may eat it; or thou mayest sell it unto an alien: for thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.

And he said unto them, This is that which the LORD hath said, To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the LORD: bake that which ye will bake to day, and seethe that ye will seethe; and that which remaineth over lay up for you to be kept until the morning.

And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.
corruption_summary: A cooking word carrying a holiness law; the modern instinct is to treat such laws as arbitrary taboo rather than as God’s claim upon common life.
corruption_paragraphs: Two mishandlings meet at the kid and the milk. The first treats the command as an unintelligible taboo, evidence that the law is primitive and safely ignored — a judgment that says more about the judge than the statute. The second overcorrects and buries the verse under a mountain of later rabbinic construction, from which the whole separation of meat and milk in kosher practice is derived. But the text is joined to the firstfruits and grounded on a single clause: thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God. The ceremonial law was never arbitrary; it was pedagogy in holiness, teaching a people at the level of the cooking pot that they belonged wholly to God, and teaching them in signs that pointed forward to Christ.

The Reformed handling is the confessional one. The ceremonial law is abrogated in Christ, who is the substance of every shadow (Col 2:16–17); the believer is not bound to the kid and the milk. But abrogation is not abolition of the principle, for the moral claim the shadow taught abides: the whole of common life stands under the Lordship of Christ, and holiness is not a Sabbath-day department. Zechariah saw the end of it — every pot in Jerusalem holiness unto the LORD of hosts, the ordinary vessel and the temple bowl at last indistinguishable. That is not the end of the law; it is the law fulfilled, when every kitchen is a sanctuary and the Canaanite is no more in the house of God.
roots_summary: To boil in liquor; the AV verb behind the kid-and-milk law and Elisha’s great pot.
roots_lines: Seethe — Saxon seōþan, “to boil”; participle sodden.
Boiling is set against roasting, the passover’s required method (Exo 12:9).
Thrice forbidden: seething a kid in his mother’s milk (Exo 23:19; 34:26; Deu 14:21).
The stated ground is holiness, not hygiene (Deu 14:21).
Zechariah’s every pot in Jerusalem shall be holiness unto the LORD (Zec 14:21).
usage: Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother’s milk — the milk of life is not the broth of death.
Bake that which ye will bake, and seethe that ye will seethe: sabbath provision made before sabbath rest.
Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage — and death in the pot met the prophet’s meal.

etymology: Rent is the old past tense and participle of rend (Saxon hrendan, to tear), and garment comes through Old French garnement, “equipment, clothing,” from garnir, to furnish. The phrase names clothing torn deliberately as a public sign.
biblical_def: Rent garments are torn clothes — the ancient, public, bodily sign of grief, horror, or protest. Jacob rends first: told his son is dead, “Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days” (Gen 37:34), and Reuben had already rent his at the empty pit (Gen 37:29). Job rends his mantle and worships in the same motion (Job 1:20). Josiah rends his clothes when the book of the law is read (2Ki 22:11), and that tearing is the beginning of a reformation. Barnabas and Paul rend theirs when Lystra would sacrifice to them (Act 14:14), for the sign serves horror at blasphemy as readily as sorrow at death. There the danger begins. The high priest was forbidden it: “he that is the high priest among his brethren…shall not uncover his head, nor rend his clothes” (Lev 21:10). Yet at the trial of Christ, “the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy” (Mat 26:65) — Caiaphas breaking the law of his own office to condemn the Lord of it, the torn robe declaring that this priesthood was finished before ever the veil was rent. Against all outward tearing stands Joel: “rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God” (Joe 2:13). Cloth is cheap; hearts are not.
webster_summary: Clothing deliberately torn as a public sign of grief, horror at blasphemy, or contrition.
webster_full: RENT, torn; parted by violence: the old participle of rend.
GARMENT, any article of clothing, as a coat, a gown, or a mantle.
To rend the garments was the eastern sign of mourning and of horror.
The high priest was expressly forbidden to rend his clothes (Lev 21:10).
Joel commands the inward tearing instead: rend your heart (Joe 2:13).
scriptures: And Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days.
Job 1:20
Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped,
Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? behold, now ye have heard his blasphemy.
Joe 2:13
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
corruption_summary: The perennial temptation is the torn coat without the torn heart — grief performed for an audience while the soul is untouched.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption of this sign is as old as the sign itself, and Joel names it: garments rent while hearts stay whole. Every age finds its own cloth to tear. Ours has made public lamentation a currency — the statement issued, the ribbon worn, the sorrow displayed before witnesses and audited by them — and the display can be total while repentance is nil. Christ marked the same instinct in men who disfigured their faces that they might appear unto men to fast (Mat 6:16). The sign is not the sin; Jacob and Job and Josiah rent honestly, and God did not despise it. The sin is the substitution: making the visible token do the work of the invisible turning, so that a man mourns for a whole nation’s wickedness and never once mourns for his own.

The high priest’s torn robe is the sharpest word here. Aaron’s successor was forbidden to rend his garments precisely because his office signified an unbroken priesthood; the anointing on his head made his very clothing holy. When Caiaphas tore his robe to charge the Son of God with blasphemy, he condemned himself twice — breaking the law of his office and calling the truth a blasphemy in the same breath — and, unwittingly, he preached. That torn robe announced the end of the Aaronic line, and within hours the veil was rent from the top to the bottom by a hand that was not a man’s (Mat 27:51). One tearing opened the way in; one tearing shut the old order out. The gospel calls not for cloth but for what Joel commanded: rend your heart, and turn unto the LORD your God.
roots_summary: Torn clothing as the AV sign of mourning, horror, and contrition — and Joel’s rebuke of it.
roots_lines: Rent — old past participle of rend, Saxon hrendan, “to tear.”
Jacob, Reuben, Job, and Josiah all rend their clothes in grief (Gen 37:29, 34; Job 1:20; 2Ki 22:11).
Apostles rend theirs in horror at attempted idolatry (Act 14:14).
The high priest was forbidden the sign (Lev 21:10); Caiaphas used it anyway (Mat 26:65).
Joel’s crown: rend your heart, and not your garments (Joe 2:13).
usage: He rent his clothes and put on sackcloth: the eastern grammar of grief.
The high priest rent his clothes — the law of his own office broken to condemn its Fulfiller.
Rend your heart, and not your garments: the only tearing God requires.

etymology: From four and score, a score being twenty — from the Saxon scoru, a notch cut on a tally stick to mark each twenty counted. Hence four twenties: eighty.
biblical_def: Fourscore is eighty — four scores, four notches of twenty on the old tally. The Authorized Version counts this way throughout, and the habit is not quaint but instructive: a score was a mark actually cut, so that biblical numbers come to us in the language of a shepherd tallying a flock he must answer for. The word gathers the men of long service. Moses “was fourscore years old, and Aaron fourscore and three years old, when they spake unto Pharaoh” (Exo 7:7) — the deliverer begins his public work at an age when the world retires him, forty years a prince, forty a shepherd, and only then sent. Barzillai the Gileadite tells David, “I am this day fourscore years old” (2Sa 19:35), and declines the king’s table with the plain dignity of a man whose senses are failing and whose loyalty is not. Moses himself sets fourscore as the outer wall of human life: “The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow” (Psa 90:10). And Anna, “a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luk 2:37), is at eighty-four the first woman to preach the newborn Christ. The number is a boundary; grace turns it into a post of duty.
webster_summary: Four times twenty; eighty — from score, a notch cut to tally each twenty.
webster_full: FOURSCORE, four times twenty; eighty.
Used also as a noun: he was fourscore.
Score is from Saxon scoru, a notch cut on a tally to mark twenty.
Moses was fourscore years old when he stood before Pharaoh (Exo 7:7).
Anna was fourscore and four when she saw the Christ (Luk 2:37).
scriptures: Exo 7:7
And Moses was fourscore years old, and Aaron fourscore and three years old, when they spake unto Pharaoh.
The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
Luk 2:37
And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.

I am this day fourscore years old: and can I discern between good and evil? can thy servant taste what I eat or what I drink? can I hear any more the voice of singing men and singing women? wherefore then should thy servant be yet a burden unto my lord the king?
corruption_summary: The score-count is dismissed as archaic clutter, and with it goes the sober reckoning of a life that must be numbered and answered for.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern versions flatten fourscore to eighty, and nothing doctrinal is lost by the arithmetic; the loss is in the picture. A score was a notch, a cut mark on a tally stick, and the counting of days in Scripture is always this sort of counting — a reckoning kept, a total that will be produced. That is why Moses ends the psalm of fourscore years with a prayer rather than a lament: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psa 90:12). Our age numbers days only to extend them; it studies longevity and avoids mortality, and a culture that cannot say fourscore has generally also stopped saying we fly away.

The second corruption is nearer home: the assumption that fourscore years is a discharge from service. Scripture nowhere retires a saint. Moses began at eighty, Caleb asked for a mountain at eighty-five (Jos 14:12), Barzillai served a fugitive king in his old age, and Anna at fourscore and four was in the temple night and day and became the first evangelist of the Incarnation to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem. Grey hairs are a crown of glory when found in the way of righteousness (Pro 16:31). The elderly saint’s strength may be labour and sorrow, but his post is not vacated until the LORD relieves him; and the church that sidelines its fourscore members has lost both its intercessors and its memory.
roots_summary: Four twenties — eighty; the AV’s tally-stick way of counting years and men.
roots_lines: Fourscore — four × score (twenty) = eighty.
Score is Saxon scoru, a notch cut on a tally stick.
Moses and Aaron were fourscore and fourscore-and-three at the exodus (Exo 7:7).
Psa 90:10 makes fourscore the outer wall of human strength.
Anna served God at fourscore and four and saw the Christ (Luk 2:37).
usage: Moses was fourscore years old when he spake unto Pharaoh — God’s servants are not retired by arithmetic.
If by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow.
A widow of about fourscore and four — and the first to speak of Him to all them that waited.

etymology: From three and score (twenty), the score being a notch cut on a tally stick to mark each twenty counted; hence three twenties: sixty. Threescore and ten is seventy.
biblical_def: Threescore is sixty, and threescore and ten is the AV’s way of saying seventy — the number that carries more covenant weight than any other in the counting. Isaac “was threescore years old” when Jacob and Esau were born (Gen 25:26). Israel goes down into Egypt as a household of seventy: “all the souls of the house of Jacob, which came into Egypt, were threescore and ten” (Gen 46:27), and that seed becomes a nation. At Elim were twelve wells and “threescore and ten palm trees” (Exo 15:27) — a wilderness picture of the tribes and the elders. Seventy elders bore the burden with Moses; seventy years Judah served Babylon; seventy weeks were determined upon the holy city (Dan 9:24); and our Lord appointed other seventy and sent them two and two before His face. Moses fixes it as the measure of a man: “The days of our years are threescore years and ten” (Psa 90:10). Over against every covenant seventy stands a counterfeit: “his number is Six hundred threescore and six” (Rev 13:18), the number of a man, falling short of the divine seven in every column. Scripture’s numbers are not magic and are not to be conjured with, but neither are they accidents; the God who names the stars keeps a tally, and every score in it is cut by His hand.
webster_summary: Three times twenty; sixty — and threescore and ten, seventy.
webster_full: THREESCORE, three times twenty; sixty.
Threescore and ten is the AV’s ordinary expression for seventy.
Score is Saxon scoru, a notch cut to mark each twenty tallied.
Seventy souls of Jacob’s house went down into Egypt (Gen 46:27).
The days of our years are threescore years and ten (Psa 90:10).
scriptures: The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
And the sons of Joseph, which were born him in Egypt, were two souls: all the souls of the house of Jacob, which came into Egypt, were threescore and ten.
And they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.
Here is wisdom. Let him that hath understanding count the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man; and his number is Six hundred threescore and six.
corruption_summary: The numbers of Scripture are handled either as meaningless or as magical; both errors dodge the plain covenant reckoning the text actually keeps.
corruption_paragraphs: One error empties the numbers. On this reading the seventy of Jacob’s house, the seventy palms at Elim, the seventy elders, the seventy years of exile, and the seventy sent out by Christ are coincidence, and to notice the pattern is to read into the text. But the text notices it: Jeremiah names the seventy years, Daniel counts them and prays, and the seventy weeks are given as an answer to that counting. The Scripture keeps a tally openly, and the reader who refuses to keep it with the Scripture will not understand Daniel at all.

The opposite error inflates them into a cipher. Numerology treats the numbers as a lock to be picked, and the number of the beast has been made to fit every enemy each generation happened to have. Yet John does not hide the meaning; he states it: it is the number of a man. Six hundred threescore and six is humanity tripled and still short — man in the place of God, falling one below the perfect seven in every column, the whole pretension of the beast summed in an arithmetic that cannot reach heaven. That is the wisdom John calls for, and it needs no secret key. The saints are numbered by name, the hairs of their head are numbered, and the number of a man will not stand against the number the Lamb has written in His book.
roots_summary: Three twenties — sixty; and threescore and ten, the covenant seventy.
roots_lines: Threescore — three × score (twenty) = sixty.
Threescore and ten = seventy, the AV’s constant idiom.
Seventy souls entered Egypt; seventy palms stood at Elim (Gen 46:27; Exo 15:27).
Threescore years and ten is the measure of a man’s days (Psa 90:10).
Six hundred threescore and six is the number of a man, not of God (Rev 13:18).
usage: The days of our years are threescore years and ten — and then we fly away.
Threescore and ten souls went down into Egypt, and a nation came out.
Six hundred threescore and six: man in the place of God, and short in every column.

etymology: From the Saxon mearg, marrow, cognate with the German Mark; the soft fatty substance within the hollow of the bones. Hence figuratively the innermost, richest, most hidden part of anything.
biblical_def: Marrow is the rich substance hidden in the hollow of the bone — the innermost, the last thing reached, the fat of the frame. Scripture uses it three ways, and each depends on the same fact: marrow is inside. First, as the measure of health. “It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones” (Pro 3:8) is Solomon’s promise to the man who fears the LORD and departs from evil; the fear of God nourishes where no physician reaches. Job describes the prosperous man whose “bones are moistened with marrow” (Job 21:24), and the sudden death of such a man is his argument that prosperity settles nothing. Second, as the measure of satisfaction. David, thirsty in a dry and weary land, says of God Himself, “My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips” (Psa 63:5) — the richest food known to him is his figure for communion with God. Isaiah takes it to the last day: the LORD of hosts shall make in this mountain “a feast of fat things full of marrow” (Isa 25:6). Third, and sharpest, as the measure of penetration. The word of God is “sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow” (Heb 4:12). Scripture reaches the marrow — the part of a man no argument, no friend, and no self-examination ever touches.
webster_summary: The soft, oleaginous substance within the bones; hence the inmost, richest part of a thing.
webster_full: MARROW, a soft, oleaginous substance contained in the cavities of animal bones.
Figuratively, the essence; the best part; the inmost substance.
From Saxon mearg; cognate with German Mark.
Solomon makes it the figure of health from the fear of the LORD (Pro 3:8).
Hebrews makes it the figure of the word’s deepest penetration (Heb 4:12).
scriptures: Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
Psa 63:5
My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips:
Isa 25:6
And in this mountain shall the LORD of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined.
Pro 3:8
It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones.
corruption_summary: The live corruption is a preaching that never reaches the marrow — Scripture handled as counsel for the surface of a life it was given to cut open.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews sets the standard and the modern pulpit often falls beneath it. The word of God is quick and powerful and divides joints from marrow; it is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. But much preaching is content to advise the joints — to adjust habits, improve homes, and manage the visible motions of a life — while the marrow is never touched. A sermon that leaves a man’s secret thoughts unexamined has not preached this book, whatever text it announced. The test is not whether the hearer was interested but whether he was found out: the word that reaches the marrow makes a man say, as the woman at the well said, He told me all things that ever I did.

Nor is the reaching merely severe. The same Scripture that pierces to the marrow offers marrow: David’s soul satisfied as with marrow and fatness, and Isaiah’s mountain feast of fat things full of marrow for all people. The knife and the banquet are the same hand. God cuts to the innermost in order to feed the innermost, and no comfort that stops short of the marrow is worth having when a man comes to die. The bones which Thou hast broken shall rejoice (Psa 51:8) — that is the whole doctrine in a line, and it is why the sharpest preaching is the kindest.
roots_summary: The fat within the bone — hence the innermost part, whether pierced or fed.
roots_lines: Marrow — Saxon mearg, the substance within the hollow of the bones.
Figuratively the inmost, richest, most hidden part of anything.
The fear of the LORD is marrow to the bones (Pro 3:8).
The soul is satisfied as with marrow and fatness in God (Psa 63:5).
The word of God divides asunder the joints and marrow (Heb 4:12).
usage: Piercing even to the dividing asunder of the joints and marrow: Scripture reaches what counsel cannot.
My soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness — the richest fare is God Himself.
A feast of fat things full of marrow: the mountain supper at the end of the world.

etymology: From the Saxon fretan, “to eat away, to devour” (for- + etan, to eat); hence to gnaw, to corrode, to wear away by rubbing — and so, of the mind, to chafe and vex itself. The AV keeps the literal sense in Lev 13:55, “it is fret inward.”
biblical_def: To fret is to gnaw — the word is literally a devouring. A garment with the plague in it “is fret inward” (Lev 13:55), eaten away beneath the surface where the eye does not reach; and that is precisely what fretting does to a soul. The great passage is the thirty-seventh Psalm, where David forbids it three times over, and each time attaches the same cause. “Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity” (Psa 37:1). “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way” (Psa 37:7). “Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil” (Psa 37:8). Solomon repeats it: “Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked” (Pro 24:19). Mark the diagnosis. Fretting is not first anxiety about tomorrow; it is envy of the prosperous wicked, the corroding suspicion that God has mismanaged the world and that the ungodly have got the better bargain. Asaph confessed the same disease and was cured only in the sanctuary, when he understood their end (Psa 73:17). Note also the reflexive: fret not thyself. A man is his own gnawer. And the cure is not a technique but a Person — rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for Him, for yet a little while and the wicked shall not be.
webster_summary: To gnaw or eat away; hence to vex, to chafe, to wear one’s self by discontent.
webster_full: FRET, to rub; to wear away by friction; to corrode.
To agitate; to vex; to make angry; and intransitively, to be vexed or chafed.
From Saxon fretan, “to eat away, devour” (for- + etan, to eat).
The AV keeps the literal sense of a garment: it is fret inward (Lev 13:55).
David thrice forbids it: fret not thyself (Psa 37:1, 7, 8).
scriptures: Psa 37:1
Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.
Psa 37:7
Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.
Psa 37:8
Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil.
Fret not thyself because of evil men, neither be thou envious at the wicked;
corruption_summary: Fretting has been reclassified as a condition to be managed rather than a sin to be mortified — and its root, envy at the prospering wicked, is never named at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Our age treats the fretting mind as a medical fact and nothing more: a state to be soothed, a matter for technique, breathing, and distraction. Scripture is far more searching and far more hopeful. It names fretting a sin — it stands in Psa 37 between anger and wrath, and it is forbidden in the imperative — and a sin can be repented of, mortified, and forgiven, which a mere condition cannot. This is not to say every troubled soul is simply rebellious; bodies break, sleep fails, and the LORD deals tenderly with dust, and He knoweth our frame. But the fretting David forbids has a doctrinal root, and no technique will pull it: it is envy at the prosperity of the wicked, which is unbelief about the government of God.

The cure Scripture gives is threefold, and every part of it is theology. First, look at the end: “for they shall soon be cut down like the grass” (Psa 37:2); Asaph could not stop fretting until he went into the sanctuary and understood their latter end. Second, rest in the LORD and wait patiently for Him — the doctrine of providence turned into a posture, believing that not one prospering wicked man escapes the Judge of all the earth. Third, do good and dwell in the land — the psalm answers idle gnawing with active duty, because a man occupied in his calling has less leisure to eat himself. Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and He shall sustain thee (Psa 55:22); the burden was never yours to carry, and the gnawing was never yours to keep.
roots_summary: To gnaw or eat away; hence to chafe with envy at the prospering wicked.
roots_lines: Fret — Saxon fretan, “to eat away, devour.”
Literal in the AV of a corroded garment: it is fret inward (Lev 13:55).
Reflexive in the Psalms: a man frets himself (Psa 37:1, 7, 8).
Its root is envy at the prosperity of the wicked, not fear of tomorrow.
Its cure is rest in the LORD and patient waiting (Psa 37:7).
usage: Fret not thyself because of evildoers — the command is reflexive; the gnawer is oneself.
It is fret inward: the plague eats the garment where no eye sees, as envy eats the soul.
Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: providence is the only cure for fretting.
